newsitem.title: USA: Trie unlikely to return to U.S. - Senate source.
newsitem.headline: Trie unlikely to return to U.S. - Senate source.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton's friend Yah Lin Trie is unlikely to return to the United States to tell a Senate probe what he knows about illegal campaign fund raising, a Senate source said on Monday.

The source said officials from the Justice Department as well as the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee had been in touch with Trie's lawyer to establish the terms under which he might return to testify.

"I don't have any indication he's going to come to the United States," the source said, adding that Trie was making unacceptable demands for immunity from criminal prosecution in exchange for his testimony.
The committee is investigating how foreign money, mostly from Asian business interests, illegally flowed into 1996 political campaigns and whether U.S. security was damaged or favours bought.
Last week the focus was on a $2.1 million loan guarantee from a Taiwanese businessman to the Republicans. This week it switches back to the Democrats.

The hearings have had little political impact, apparently because the material is complicated and the names unfamiliar. But the committee has already unearthed considerable evidence of the way the parties, especially the Democrats, engaged in a desperate chase for campaign funds, paying scant attention to legal niceties.
Trie, a former Little Rock restaurant owner and a friend of Clinton's when the president was governor of Arkansas, will be the focus of Senate hearings this week.

He, along with his wife and company, gave $202,000 to the Democratic Party from 1994 to 1996 and $600,000 to Clinton's Presidential Legal Expense Trust. The money was subsequently returned when it became clear it came from overseas.

Trie took refuge in China when the investigations began and has refused to respond to subpoenas. But he surfaced last weekend in an ABC interview, saying he might return to the United States as early as this week and had nothing to hide.
"I'm not hiding. I want to stay alive. I want to make my own business. The past is the past," Trie said.
The Senate source said the committee had no interest in providing Trie with a platform for denials. He would have to provide records of his activities under oath.
Failing that, Trie might be interviewed by committee investigators overseas, the source said.

The hearings, now in their fourth week, are expected to begin with testimony about how Trie formed an association with a Macau-based Chinese national named Ng Lap Sing, who was apparently the source of his money.
"During this period, Trie did not appear to have any legitimate business of any kind," the source said.
Testimony would trace $1 million from Ng's Bank of China account in Hong Kong to Trie, from which it was funnelled to various Democratic or Clinton-associated accounts.
The committee will also hear from two Asian-American housewives who were unwittingly involved in a money-laundering scheme involving cash transmitted from Ng to the Democratic Party.
The two women, relatives of an employee of Ng's, wrote checks for $25,000 so he could attend a Feb. 19,1996, fund-raising event in Washington addressed by Clinton.
